items.title: Government, Landbridge rift over Darwin Port deepens as dispute action looms
paras: Landbridge has reiterated it will be going ahead with international legal action over Darwin Port. ( ABC News: Che Chorley )
Anthony Albanese suggests negotiations are continuing with Landbridge over its Darwin Port lease, but the Chinese-owned company refutes that.
The union representing port workers says it wants to see the dispute resolved.

The rift between the federal government and the Chinese-owned company that holds a 99-year lease over the Port of Darwin has deepened after Landbridge reiterated it will be going ahead with a formal dispute under the Australia-China Free Trade Agreement.

In Shenzhen in China yesterday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told reporters he was determined the federal government would go ahead with its election commitment to either acquire the Darwin Port lease or ensure it was sold to an Australian company, to return it to Australian hands before the next election.
Anthony Albanese says the government is determined the port will be returned to "Australian hands". ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore )
"We've made clear our position, which is that Darwin Port should stay in Australian hands, it should never have been sold," he said.
"There might be legal consequences and actions we are continuing to pursue.
"We've made our position very clear that we want to sell or buy the asset."
Mr Albanese also suggested that negotiations over his government's plan were taking place.
Anthony Albanese says the government has made its position "very clear". ( ABC News: Michael Franchi )
"The owners, Landbridge, are engaging and there are discussions taking place," he said.
"But Landbridge are not ruling out taking action in terms of international tribunals as well."
The NT's previous Country Liberal Party (CLP) government sold Landbridge the Darwin Port lease in 2015 to raise $500 million, to ease its burgeoning debt position.
The lease has become the subject of intense geopolitical debate in the decade since.
The Darwin Port lease was sold to Landbridge in 2015 by the NT government at the time. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi )
In April, Landbridge lodged a case with the World Bank's International Centre for Settlement of Investor Disputes, requesting "arbitration proceedings".
In a statement issued late yesterday, Landbridge sought to refute the prime minister's suggestion about negotiations.
"Landbridge denies that it has engaged with the Commonwealth in any commercial discussions or negotiations in relation to the divestment of the lease of the Port of Darwin," the statement said.
"Landbridge has at all times made it clear to the Commonwealth that it was not a willing seller of the port and does not intend to enter any commercial negotiations … for the sale of the port."
Landbridge reiterated it was going ahead with its World Bank formal dispute.
"Landbridge was left with no alternative but to take steps to protect its legal rights and lodge a formal dispute under the Australia-China Free Trade Agreement," the company said in its statement.
Terry O'Connor is Landbridge's non-executive director in Australia. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi )
Landbridge also said it hoped the federal government would not make moves to strip it of the port while the international action was underway.

"Landbridge … expects that the Commonwealth will not take any steps in breach of its international law commitments and allow Landbridge the opportunity for its claim to be properly heard and determined in accordance with the commitments made by the Commonwealth under the Australia-China FTA," the statement said.
Asked for his view on the stoush, NT Treasurer Bill Yan provided a statement in which he said the NT government was trying to help the Commonwealth.
"This is a federal government commitment to return the Darwin Port to Australian hands," he said.
"We are working closely with the Commonwealth to achieve that end. We need a decision soon to provide certainty."
China progressively lifted its prohibitive tariffs on Australian beef, barley, wine, coal, timber and lobster during 2024 and 2023 as relations between Australia and the country thawed.
Since then the relationship has fluctuated over human rights, activity in the South China Sea and other issues.

Asked whether his sector was worried the dispute over the port could sour Australia-China relations , the chief executive of the NT Livestock Exporters Association, Patrick Moran, said: "That's a matter for the Chinese and Australian governments."
"They're not interested in getting involved in the politics of this issue."
Andy Burford says the infrastructure at Darwin Port needs upgrading. ( ABC News: Jane Bardon )
Maritime Union of Australia NT branch secretary Andy Burford said workers at the Darwin Port "would like a bit of certainty which way it's going to go".
"Since the transfer they have just been getting on with their jobs," he said.
"To them it's business as usual, but of course they're concerned about it, and they'd like to see it all sorted."
Mr Burford said rather than spending money bringing a dispute in an international tribunal, workers would like to see more investment go into continuing to upgrade the port's infrastructure.
"We need more docks for the tugs, all the infrastructure is getting older now, so the upkeep of it all is an expensive situation. So that's what we need the money to be spent on," he said.

items.title: Miners slump, weighing down ASX as unemployment hits five-year high
paras: Advertisement Updated Business Markets World markets Miners slump, weighing down ASX as unemployment hits five-year high Staff writers Updated November 19, 2026 — 5:18pm , first published November 19, 2026 — 5:17am
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Share A A A The Australian sharemarket’s losing streak continued on Thursday, with the local bourse falling for a sixth straight session and wiping out the rest of this year’s gains as global AI anxiety weighed on the mining and tech sectors and Australia reported its highest unemployment rate since 2021.

The S&P/ASX 200 closed 91.40 points, or 1 per cent, lower at 8730.40, basically flat from its level at the start of the year. Mining heavyweights led the losses after the price of copper, seen as integral to the AI boom, plunged by almost 6 per cent overnight. The Australian dollar slid 0.5 per cent to $US66.86¢, also wiping out its gains for the year, on the back of the weak employment data.

Global markets are on an unsteady footing as doubts over AI companies hover. AP The newly created AFR Real Economy index – which tracks 500 companies that mirror the ABS’ composition of the actual economy– was down 0.5 per cent, while the AFR Global 50, which tracks Australia’s top 50 companies with majority revenue from offshore, slumped 1.4 per cent.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics’ labour force data showed the Reserve Bank’s aggressive tightening of monetary policy has hit the jobs market, with the unemployment rate spiking to 4.9 per cent last month. Unemployment rose by 0.2 percentage points, reaching its highest level since 2021.

The weaker-than-expected labour market reinforced bets that the RBA has ended its interest-rate hike cycle and will pivot to cuts next year, sending the Aussie dollar to its lowest since early January.
“This release all but closes the door on a December hike and shifts the debate to how long rates stay at their peak,” said Sunny Nguyen, head of the Australian economics team at Moody’s Analytics.

While prospects of an interest rate reprieve usually boost sentiment, it wasn’t enough to dispel dark clouds over the AI trade, which has been driving global markets this year and is faltering amid fears the heavily indebted and interdependent sector could also make them crash.

Despite those concerns, AI frontier lab Anthropic – the company behind chatbot Claude – released the pricing for its Wall Street float. Bloomberg said the stock will be set at $US83 per share, above its target range of $US70 to $US78, valuing the company at $US1.5 trillion ($2.2 trillion). The company is set to start trading on Friday morning (AEDT).

Mining stocks plunged yet again on the ASX, with BHP down another 3.7 per cent and Rio Tinto down 4.1 per cent. Copper steadied after plunging almost 6 per cent overnight – the biggest drop since April 2025 – on a sharp unwinding of bullish bets tied to AI and US tariffs. The red metal has lost 12 per cent so far in November, fuelled by growing doubts over the durability of AI-related spending and fading expectations for US tariffs on refined copper.

Gold miners also extended losses, with Northern Star slumping 5.7 per cent, Evolution Mining plunging 7.3 per cent and Newmont down 4.6 per cent. Gold wavered near a 14-month low after Federal Reserve officials signalled its interest-rate hikes are likely to stretch into next year, making the non-yielding metal less attractive for investors.
Financial stocks were holding up better, with Commonwealth Bank up 0.4 per cent, while Westpac dropped 0.2 per cent, ANZ Bank slipped 0.1 per cent and National Australia Bank dropped 0.9 per cent.

Energy stocks finished lower, with Woodside Energy down 2 per cent, Santos down 1.9 per cent and refiner Ampol down 2.7 per cent. Oil had slumped overnight, but steadied as traders assessed the outlook for the US-Iran conflict, including the possibility of fresh attacks against Tehran, with Brent holding above $US92 a barrel. US President Donald Trump is weighing plans for further strikes, the New York Times reported, citing US and Israeli officials. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing him to join a four- to seven-day campaign, it said.

Technology stocks were mixed, with local AI-related stocks NextDC and Megaport up 4.3 per cent and 3.5 per cent following Anthropic’s higher-than-expected IPO price. Software maker WiseTech dropped 0.9 per cent and Xero was flat.

In New York trading, the S&P 500 dragged Wall Street to its longest losing streak since June, with AI stocks continuing to weigh on global indexes. The S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent after zigzagging between gains and losses through the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite added 0.4 per cent.

Nvidia was once again at the centre of Wall Street’s moves. Its stock initially jumped 2.7 per cent after the chip company reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, but that gain was wiped out and it closed 2.9 per cent lower. Perhaps more importantly, it also gave a forecast for revenue in the current quarter that was better than expected.

The question is whether Nvidia’s big growth can continue despite the turmoil created by the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. He had an immense personality that drew attention and investment to AI, and he built Nvidia into a company so big that it helped to fund some of the industry’s growth itself.

“Our momentum is real,” Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, told investors and financial analysts after announcing the company’s latest results. “Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us. And employees are committed. We’ve got this.”
The encouraging numbers and words coming from Nvidia failed to create lasting gains for the price of its stock or for others across the industry.

items.title: Cheap Chinese EVs are causing havoc on the Australian used car market
paras: Used cars are losing value faster as EVs and Chinese manufacturing reshape the global car industry. ( Getty: fotog )
Petrol cars (excluding hybrids of all kinds) lost five times more value in 2026 than the previous year.
Diesel SUVs also steeply declined in value, but utes and large four-wheel drives fared better.
Experts say some used petrol and diesel cars may become hard to sell due to competition from low-cost new EVs.
More used cars are for sale; they are selling for less, and petrol cars are losing value fastest.
These are insights from the latest industry data showing the impact of low-cost Chinese EVs on a second-hand car market dominated by petrol and diesel vehicle sales.
Dealerships are struggling to shift stock and say conditions are the "worst ever".
Some in the industry believe the value of used fossil fuel vehicles will continue to decline as EVs get cheaper and buyers look to save on fuel.
Although new-car sales get the most attention, most Australians buy their cars on the second-hand market.
In 2026, changes in the new-car market rippled through auction houses, dealerships and online marketplaces that shift over 2 million used cars every year.
The war in Iran and high fuel prices, along with an influx of low-cost, heavily discounted Chinese brands, drove a surge in new EV sales .
As EV uptake increased, used petrol and diesel vehicles flooded the second-hand market.
New Chinese SUVs were advertised for the typical asking price of a three-year-old Toyota Rav4, Steven Bragg, a motor industry adviser at Pitcher Partners, told the ABC.
"The Chinese SUV probably has better tech, better specs, and a new car warranty of eight years," he said.
He said dealerships found themselves stuck with stock that was rapidly losing value.
The Australian Automotive Dealers Association (AADA) wants to stop new brands entering the market.
"It's becoming more difficult to value some vehicles on the used car market because such is the rate of change," AADA chief executive James Voortman said.
Australians prefer to buy their cars second-hand, making the used-car market about twice the size of the new-car one. ( ABC News: John Gunn )
Used cars always depreciate, but now some models are losing value faster than before.
Petrol cars (excluding hybrids and plug-in hybrids) lost five times more value in 2026 than in the previous year, according to data from the analytics platform AutoGrab.

Diesels lost about twice as much value in 2026 as hybrids and battery-electric vehicles, with SUVs faring worse than utes and four-wheel drives designed for heavy towing, data from online used car dealership Carma shows.
Some say this is the market correcting itself after used cars became overpriced during the pandemic.
Variables affecting depreciation rates include fuel prices and electric alternatives, inflation, and broader cost-of-living pressures.
"Most of the key industry data sources say it's likely used car prices will continue to fall for the foreseeable future," Mike Costello, an industry analyst at Cox Automotive, told the ABC.
He said demand for used diesel utes and large four-wheel drives should remain robust while there are few EV equivalents.
The EV industry's peak body, the EV Council, made a similar prediction.
"Demand for certain vehicle segments is going to evaporate and may evaporate quicker than people expect," EVC head of policy Aman Gaur said.

"I would just urge people who are buying petrol cars to be cautious about what the future demand might be, given the demand for petrol cars is decreasing, and the demand for electric cars is increasing."
Market segments already well served by EVs include hatchbacks, sedans and mid-size SUVs. ( ABC News: John Gunn )
Sales of new petrol cars (excluding hybrids) have almost halved over six years.
But Fleet News director Marc Sibbald dismissed the idea Australians would flock to EVs.
"In five years time we'll still be struggling with charging infrastructure," Mr Sibbald said.
"There'll still be non-believers. There's my neighbour who thinks BYD is spying on them, the guys I drink with at the pub who think EVs are going to catch on fire."
He advises fleet managers that petrol and diesel cars will depreciate at the long-term average rate.
Brendon Green, a general manager at Pickles Auctions, said fossil fuel vehicle resale values would not collapse.
"We anticipate a gradual shift in resale values rather than a dramatic decline, with the extent of any price movements varying across vehicle segments."
Used EVs tend to depreciate much faster than used fossil fuel cars, losing about half their value over three years.
The spike in EV demand in March meant they temporarily gained value, but industry data shows they are now losing value again.
Cox Automotive's Mr Costello expected EVs would hold their value better as fears about severe battery degradation proved unfounded.
" We're seeing cars with 90–95 per cent of battery health remaining entering the second-hand market," he said.
The influx of low-cost Chinese brands in 2026 was the result of a combination of events that may not be repeated, Carma chief executive Lachlan MacGregor said.
Chinese domestic sales slumped, causing manufacturers to expand overseas just as the United States, Europe and Canada banned or limited vehicle imports.
"We've had the fierce forces of competition like no other market has had," he said.
The price of EVs in five years will depend largely on battery prices, which in turn depend on research outcomes and manufacturing advances that are hard to predict.
Another variable is what models manufacturers make available in Australia.
Small EVs with limited range are being sold in China for less than $10,000.
Mr Bragg said a car like this in the Australian market could collapse the value of used hatchbacks, but only if buyers thought it was as good as petrol models.
"If it's a Corolla-level-good vehicle for a great price, then 100 per cent it would impact the market."

items.title: Could modern Australians be as brutal as our Anzacs?
paras: Are you getting sick and tired of the limp nonsense coming out of the left? I am.
One leftist article in a leftist rag went on and on about the ‘militarisation’ of Remembrance Day and Anzac Day and the absence of the ‘frontier wars’ in the ‘narrative’.

What really bothers me is that the fearless sons and daughters of Anzacs have a reputation to protect. Meanwhile, the leftists are actively trying to undermine that fearsome reputation among our younger generation.
The Desert Fox, Erwin Rommel, arguably one of the greatest generals in history, wrote of the Australians he encountered, coincidentally on Anzac Day 1941:

‘…some 50 or 60 Australian prisoners were marched off close beside us – immensely big and powerful men, who without question represented an élite formation of the British Empire, a fact that was also evident in battle. Enemy resistance was as stubborn as ever…’
Rommel also described the Australians at Tobruk in 1941 as fighting with outstanding tenacity, with even wounded men continuing to fire.
‘The Australian troops are fighting magnificently and their training is far superior to ours.’
‘Fierce fighting followed with the Australians, whom we knew only too well from the time of the Tobruk siege, and lasted well into the night.’

Rommel also reportedly ranked Australians highly as individual soldiers while noting they could be rough (especially toward Italians) and potentially difficult to command in very large numbers. (This is something that Anthony Albanese is discovering.)

In the Great War, the Anzacs established a reputation as disciplined and brutal trench raiders. Aggressive patrolling remains an Australian tactic that differs most notably from the approaches of American soldiers.

A ‘clearing patrol’ by US soldiers in the Vietnam War consisted of a platoon letting loose a hail of lead into the platoon’s vicinity. Australians would instead walk the ground, silently, spaced out to avoid casualties from being too bunched together. Much more dangerous, to be sure, but much cheaper for a nation that lacks the logistics capacity of the greatest military force in history. But that’s not what I wanted to discuss.

During the Great War, Australian troops conducted trench raids. These were typically small-scale and consisted of 6 to 12 soldiers armed with hand-to-hand melee weapons like nail-studded clubs (known as knobkerries), brass knuckledusters, trench knives, hatchets, and Mills bombs. The idea was to infiltrate the enemy’s trenches, gather intelligence and prisoners, and no doubt to scare the living hell out of the Germans.
The Anzacs would slip out silently under the cover of darkness, creep past barbed wire and forward posts, and breach the enemy lines.
The goal was to disrupt enemy morale, destroy dugouts, sabotage machine-gun nests, gather intelligence documents, and capture prisoners for interrogation before retreating back to friendly lines.

Instead, we have leftists wanting to be peaceful while our enemies are taking advantage of our cowardice. Or suggesting that we could have pretended we were not part of the British Empire or now the Free World. Talk about being a free rider!

Sometimes the raiding parties were supported by fighting patrols. I commanded a couple of fighting patrols in training. It was basically a two-section platoon with two MAG58 section machine guns and riflemen. Apparently, the half-platoon fighting patrol concept developed during the first world war with Lewis guns.

(The MAG58 was my favourite machine gun. It is a tool like a crowbar. Hard on the hands and hard to work, yet extremely effective. The infantry battalions I later worked with had them modified with the M60’s bipod. Much more robust than the standard pressed aluminium bipod. But I digress.)

For what it is worth, the fighting patrol has less firepower than a platoon, but it is far more manoeuvrable. Combat power typically consists of firepower, manoeuvrability, and morale. Now imagine you are facing a bunch of enormous Anzacs with nailed clubs, supported by a fighting patrol, and with the moral backing of their families and nation…
When facing these Anzacs, the Germans were in a state of constant anxiety. This night-raiding discipline and brutality continued for decades after. Any wonder Rommel was impressed!

Which brings me to today. I have Facebook ‘friends’ who have made a sport out of being two-tier Facebook police. They defend the recent comments by the UN’s Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. He comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and is currently lecturing Australia on ‘embarrassing’ Indigenous incarceration standards.

His own country’s record on violence against women, children, and civilians is exponentially worse than Australia’s, with a far weaker state that is unwilling to address its own problems. Please don’t let me confuse you with my facts!

The Australian left’s critique of the so-called ‘militarisation’ of Remembrance Day and Anzac Day neglects the fact that they can say the things they can because the Anzacs put themselves on the line, and even behind the lines, to preserve their freedom, even to be idiots.

But these two-tier tentacles need to be removed from the story of our Anzacs. And to charges that these commemorative days are supported by ‘unquestionable sacred/religious grandeur (and marked with Christian prayer)’? They’re right.
I doubt there were many atheists in the trenches on the Western Front. Those who didn’t pay with their lives paid with their sanity. War is hell, after all.

Freedom is not retained by people who flinch at the memory of what it once required. If modern Australians cannot stomach the reputation its Anzacs earned, it should at least stop pretending it earned the peace they left behind.
Dr Michael de Percy @FlaneurPolitiq is the Spectator Australia’s Canberra Press Gallery Correspondent. If you’d like to support his writing, please shout him a drink over at Donorbox .

items.title: Cummins’ ad dollars on the line as Sandpapergate hits sponsors
paras: Advertisement Exclusive Business Companies Ball tampering Cummins’ ad dollars on the line as Sandpapergate hits sponsors Elias Visontay November 19, 2026 — 7:02pm
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Share A A A Corporations that have spent millions to attach their brands to the credibility of Australian captain Pat Cummins and the national cricket team are staring down the barrel of not being able to market their expensive sponsorships as the ball tampering scandal engulfs the sport, experts warn.
A key charity has pulled ads featuring Cummins after online comments shifted into discussion of the team’s troubles, distracting from the charity’s appeal.

Pat Cummins trained at the Sydney Cricket Ground ahead of the NSW Blues match against Queensland on Sunday. Kate Geraghty “We temporarily paused the older campaign advertisement after comments shifted away from the campaign and towards recent reporting about Australian cricket,” a UNICEF spokeswoman said, while noting Cummins remained an unpaid ambassador for the Australian arm of the charity.

Cummins has insisted he knew nothing of a plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper during the 2018 tour of South Africa. Other team members have stated the whole team knew, sending Australian cricket into crisis.

Cummins is Australia’s top-earning cricketer with an estimated income of between $9 million and $10 million a year. He rejected a roughly $10 million a year offer to play T20 cricket exclusively last year.

Contracts with Cricket Australia and the Indian Premier League pay Cummins about $3 million each, this masthead has previously reported . The remaining millions come from other sources, including sponsorship deals with local and international brands.

The list of sponsors is long. Sportwear giant New Balance has sponsored Cummins since 2011 as part of a deal to promote the label’s cricket and training gear. Razor brand Gilette, owned by multinational Procter & Gamble, pays Cummins to be a “brand ambassador”, including spruiking its shaving and grooming products and appearing in promotional videos.

The 33-year-old is also a brand ambassador for retail tech giant Amazon’s Prime Video streaming service, under a deal which sees him promote the platform’s live ICC cricket coverage – including performing a stand-up comedy-style routine earlier this year – as well as appearing in other ads for the site.

He also has endorsement agreements with sports streaming platform Kayo, as well as with Carrera Eyewear, and has previously appeared in a campaign for Tourism Australia. Big four bank Westpac also counts Cummins as an ambassador and has used him in advertising campaigns.
Cummins’ individual sponsorships exist in tandem with a landmark sponsorship of the Australian men’s team and Cricket Australia, reportedly worth $40 million over four years.

Westpac took over from rival bank Commonwealth, which let its sponsorship lapse. After the 2018 sandpaper revelations, CBA focused its sponsorship on women’s cricket for the final years of its deal, which expired last year. Toyota, NRMA Insurance and Origin Energy also sponsor the team.
Most major sponsors were silent on the saga when contacted by this masthead.

Toyota remains committed to its partnership with Cricket Australia, saying it “continues to support the organisation as it works to resolve this matter”. NRMA said its partnership with cricket continued and it supported “steps being taken to give those involved the opportunity to be heard”.
However, branding experts said sponsors were most likely already carefully considering their next moves.

Adam Ferrier, a creative strategist and founder of advertising firm Thinkerbell, said that, while cricket’s broad influence was a key appeal for sponsors, and though its popularity was unlikely to change as a result of the current scandal, another key factor, and sore point, was reputation.
He said the Australian cricket team and the captain were a shorthand for how we feel about the country.

“Even though it’s just cricket, it’s about all of us,” Ferrier said. “If this keeps on going, there’ll come a time when this will significantly impact the commercial value of cricket and the players involved because brands just won’t want to be associated with it.”

Steve Allen, media analyst and managing director of Fusion Strategy, said Cummins’ reputation and sponsorship value were at greatest risk not just because he was current captain, but because he had spoken in such certain terms.
“[Cummins] has outright denied knowledge ... if he has even told a white lie, he is toast to sponsors and for life he will have irreparably damaged his reputation.
“If I was advising a major sponsor I would recommend pausing,” he said. “This would be devastating for him because he is seen as a total clean skin, a white knight.”

Allen said the value Cummins or Cricket Australia could demand from future sponsorship deals would probably take a hit from the saga so far. “I would want to know what else is being hidden, what else are you not telling us that could be a risk for us and our brand and that’s why they’d say the next deal would be a decrease not an increase.
“They hook their horse to the wagon to get that golden halo ... Usually, they do it for reputational enhancement, but here we’re facing reputational corrosion,” Allen said.

Ben Willee, executive director of the agency Spinach Advertising, believed sponsors were already making contingency plans, noting former prime minister John Howard’s famous quip that the Australian men’s cricket captain was the nation’s most important job.

“Most people would be surprised how nervous the sponsors are right now,” he said. “All of a sudden you’re not associated with a beloved sportsperson but you’re associated with a possible cheat and that’s a bad thing for a brand.
“This is a moral issue and it’s not going away because it’s clear there are two camps saying completely different things.
“You want to be associated with someone accused of cheating about as much as you want to buy a timeshare at a resort in Chernobyl,” Willee said.

items.title: ED arrests six persons in cross-border drugs smuggling network
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): The Enforcement Directorate ( ED ) has arrested six persons in connection with an investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) case linked to a cross-border drug smuggling network, the agency said on Tuesday. ED 's Delhi unit arrested these accused in different operations launched on October 11, October 18 and October 20. The arrested accused are identified as Lovejit Singh alias Labba, Manjeet Singh alias Manna, Prabhjit Singh, Gurjot Singh, Ramandeep Singh, and Gurpreet Singh. "A major drug trafficking operation involving smuggling of heroin from Afghanistan into India was unearthed during investigation," said the ED in a statement. The PMLA investigation was initiated on the basis of seizure of 293.81 kg of heroin from containers imported by Sandhu Exports at Nhava Sheva Port by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence and seizure of 352.71 kg of heroin from two vehicles and a flat in Faridabad, Haryana, by the Delhi Police Special Cell. Thus, a total of 646.52 kg of heroin has been seized so far. ED investigation revealed that the arrested persons, Lovejit Singh, Manjeet Singh, Ramandeep Singh, Gurjot Singh, Gurpreet Singh and Prabhjit Singh, coordinated the smuggling, storage and distribution of heroin across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi.

"These individuals were key members of a syndicate that smuggled heroin from Afghanistan and Iran, concealing them within shipments of talc stone and gypsum powder," said the ED . Accused persons incorporated Sandhu Exports, a front company owned by Prabhjit Singh, to carry out the smuggling of drugs, informed the federal agency. ED uncovered the highly sophisticated heroin smuggling and money laundering network where identification of multiple bank accounts, cash transactions, and operational expenses by the accused has been made. "Accused disguised the origin of the illicit funds, which were further layered and integrated into seemingly legitimate financial activities. It was also revealed that the syndicate did not make any payments to Afghan suppliers until the drugs were sold in local markets." Further, the agency said the accused used cash payments to purchase multiple vehicles including Toyota Fortuner, Etios and Hyundai Verna etc in second hand market for trafficking from the storage Hubs to further distribution. The ED investigation revealed that cash was used for the purchase of high-end smartphones and encrypted communication apps were used to coordinate smuggling activities. "Drugs smuggled from Iran and Afghanistan used to be imported via the Nava Sheva port in Mumbai, later stored at a rented godown in Shivpuri, Madhya Pradesh and further distributed for local supply in parts of Delhi, Punjab and Haryana. Transportation was carried out in lesser quantities of 10 kg to prevent detection by law enforcement agencies. Earlier, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits have been attached by ED ," added the agency. (ANI)

items.title: Asia's Largest Mindfulness India Summit 2024 Marks a New Era for Corporate Culture and Personal Well-being with the Inau
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel PNN Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: The Mindfulness India Summit 2024, an initiative by the Mindful Science Centre, presented by HSBC and supported by CII Leadership and HR Committee, successfully concluded its two-day event on October 17 and 18, 2024, establishing new benchmarks in corporate culture and personal well-being. With over 40 international and national experts addressing mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and neuroscience, the summit highlighted how these principles are essential in transforming leadership, enhancing employee engagement, and fostering sustainable well-being within organizations. The evolving workplace landscape, particularly the increasing role of AI, requires a renewed focus on human-centric leadership and emotional resilience. The summit provided a platform for forward-thinking leaders to explore how mindfulness can effectively bridge this gap, ensuring both corporate excellence and employee well-being . The summit featured MasterChef Sanjeev Kapoor as the Chief Guest, who shared how mindful leadership has played a pivotal role in building his culinary empire. Along with Chris Ruane, Ex MP British Parliament and Chair of Mindfulness Initiative UK, J N Behl and Global Holistic Health Guru Mickey Mehta, Kapoor also launched Manish Behl's new book "Observe - 101 Mindfulness Practices", a guide designed to make mindfulness accessible for both professionals and individuals in their everyday lives. Behl, a global mindfulness expert and founder of the Mindful Science Centre, shared, "With this book, I want to demystify mindfulness and make it accessible to everyone. Mindfulness is not a complex or distant concept, but a practical tool for reducing stress, improving focus, and fostering deeper connections in both personal and professional settings." The Mindfulness India Summit 2024 has successfully proven that mindfulness is no longer a luxury but a necessity in modern corporate structures. By adopting mindfulness practices, organizations are not only creating more compassionate work environments but are also enhancing their overall performance and sustainability in a world increasingly shaped by technological and emotional complexity. The 2 days also saw the launch of Mindfulness Impact Awards, to honor organizations and individuals who have integrated mindfulness into their corporate structures and personal lives. These awards reflect the growing recognition that workplace culture directly affects employee productivity, creativity, and overall well-being. Manish Behl, founder of the awards, explained, "Corporate success today goes beyond profit; it's about fostering environments where employees thrive mentally, emotionally, and physically. Our vision with these awards is to inspire a deeper integration of mindfulness in corporate cultures worldwide. By recognizing these pioneers, we hope these awards inspire companies and individuals to further integrate mindfulness into their environments, ultimately fostering happier, more productive workplaces, communities, and a more compassionate world." The awards were designed to acknowledge champions of mindfulness across categories, recognizing those who incorporate mindful practices to improve workplace culture, employee engagement, and societal impact. Winners ranged from corporate giants like Aditya Birla Group and Accenture to global educators and community leaders. Award Winners Include: - Entrepreneur: Mickey Mehta (India) - Commitment: Aditya Birla Group, Accenture (India) - Champions: IPG Mediabrands (India) - Communities: HPCL (India) - Champions: Hincolas (India)

- Creativity: Siemens (India) - Entrepreneur (Global): Michael Bunting (Australia) - Educator (Global): Susan Reynolds (USA) - Champion (Global): Dr. Urszula Klich (USA) - Communities (Global): Iva Mia Kruslin (Croatia) - Creativity (Global): Dr. Chris Reina (USA) - Educator (Global): Geshe la Lakhdor (India) - Communities (Global): Chris Ruane - Mindfulness Initiative UK Picture Caption - L to R: Chris Ruane, Mindfulness Initiative UK, J N Behl, father of Manish Behl, Manish Behl, Global Mindfulness Expert, Masterchef Sanjeev Kapoor and Mickey Mehta, Global Holistic Health Guru Media Contact: - Usha Rachael Thomas - Cell: India - +919821382227 / UAE - +971509058213 About Mindful Science Centre: The Mindful Science Centre is India's leading global institution focused on integrating mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and neuroscience into leadership and workplace practices. items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: "India matters most for future of planet" says British High Commissioner Lindy Cameron
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): In recent times when climate change has become a pressing issue with countries across the world being ravaged due to climate catastrophes, it becomes imperative to discuss and deliberate upon global actions that can help the world rise up and meet these challenges. At the NDTV World Summit's a discussion was held on the theme, "India Matters The Most For Future Of Planet". Participants in the discussion included Erik Solheim, Former Minister of Climate and the Environment of Norway; Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India; Shishir Priyadarshi, President Chintan Research Foundation; Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative. "India is the country that matters the most for the future of the planet and climate change. India's ambition for development should not in any way be constrained by the responsibilities of the planet," Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India, emphasised. She noted that the UK is committed towards the Multilateral Development Banks (MDB) reforms, technology and research support in India to aid the efforts. "Every dollar invested in resilient infrastructure pays 4 times over," said Cameron. "Lived experience of climate emergencies helps people to understand why their government needs to take policy action now," she added. Further talking about the need for urgent government action, Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative said, "Series of disasters affecting both developed and developing countries are serving as a wake-up call. As rich countries will get more and more affected by climate change which they did not imagine till a couple of years ago, most vulnerable countries are going to be struggling with impacts who also have very less capacity to deal with it. India is taking a leadership role in the global fight against climate change. Initiatives such as Global Biofuels Alliance, International Solar Alliance, and Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure are some efforts taken by India in recent years to manage the climate crisis. (ANI)

items.title: India to grow at 6.8 pc in FY25 and 6.6 pc in FY26: S&P Global Market Intelligence
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): India's growth, although moderating, remains strong with a forecasted average of 6.8 per cent for the fiscal year 2024-25 and 6.6 per cent for 2025-26, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence . Despite a slowdown in economic momentum due to weaker public-sector investment, the outlook for India's economy is buoyed by several positive factors. Easing inflation, favourable monsoon conditions, and increased government social spending are expected to boost household demand. Additionally, healthy corporate balance sheets are playing a vital role in supporting the recovery of private investment. S&P Global Market Intelligence has released its October Global Economic Forecast update, emphasizing a steady global economic expansion supported by policy stimulus, while acknowledging risks from geopolitical factors. The outlook highlights moderating inflation and easing monetary policies as key factors steering the global economy towards a "soft landing."

Ken Wattret, global economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence , remarked, "The global economy is on track for a soft landing, with inflation rates moderating and monetary policy easing becoming more widespread. Still, geopolitical developments have the capacity to dampen or even derail the expansion." Report forecasts an annual real GDP growth rate of 4.3 per cent in 2024 and 4.4 per cent in 2025 for the region excluding China and Japan. Aiding this growth is resilient domestic demand, as regional central banks adopt more accommodative monetary stances. The start of the US Federal Reserve's easing cycle in September is creating more room for interest rate cuts, prompting several central banks, including those in the Philippines, New Zealand, Hong Kong SAR, and Indonesia, to lower rates. S&P Global Market Intelligence underscores that while the global economic outlook remains positive, risks persist. Geopolitical tensions could potentially derail economic progress, especially in regions with heightened uncertainties. Nonetheless, policy measures aimed at stimulating growth, coupled with moderating inflation, are setting the stage for a sustained economic expansion. (ANI)

items.title: "No shortage of oil in world and prices should hopefully come down", says Hardeep Singh Puri
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Hardeep Singh Puri, Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas on Tuesday said that there is no shortage of oil in the world and prices will come down soon, answering the question of the recent upswing in crude oil prices. Speaking to the media, the Union Minister cited global factors such as the war in the Middle East and voluntary cuts in oil production which are influencing the oil prices in the global market. He said, "It depends on global factors. One thing is very clear, there is no shortage of oil in the world...Today, more and more oil is coming on the market...There are other factors like geopolitical tensions. So, there is no shortage of oil but if there is tension in one part of the world, then the freight cost, and insurance freight cost will go up. Today, let us all hope that better sense prevails, that call for peace that our Prime Minister has been making from every forum...There is more than enough oil in the world and prices should hopefully come down. That's my expectation..." "If there's tension in one part of the world, then the cost of, if you have to take a longer route, then the cost of the freight cost, the insurance rate cost, that will go up...There's more than enough oil in the world, and prices should hopefully come down," he commented in his personal capacity.

The union minister said many countries such as Brazil, and Guayana among others are coming with their oil. Citing the stable prices in the last 3 years, the minister said that the government is taking every possible step to ensure stable oil prices. "Central government at every stage has stepped in to cushion and bring the prices down from November 2021 to May 2022. Now there are some global factors. The cost at the retail point is determined by the cost of the barrel in the international market plus the cost of transportation, freight, insurance, retailers, refining cost and margin, then dealers, margin, etc. We are solving all the problems we can, now you tell the global community to hold and bring them down," he added. This comes after oil prices rose nearly 2 per cent on Monday, reclaiming major losses from last week's sell-off. Brent crude features upped by $1.44, or 1.97 per cent in the afternoon. Earlier this month, Puri had said that the country is well-prepared to meet its growing energy demands, with a diverse range of oil sources. Speaking on the availability of oil in the global market, Puri emphasised that India has expanded its procurement base, moving from 27 suppliers to 39. (ANI)

items.title: How aquanauts could help save Florida’s reefs
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print It sounds idyllic. Who wouldn’t want to occupy a newly built residence in the Florida Keys, complete with its own coral garden right outside the window? The only complication is that it is 17 metres below the surface of the Atlantic Ocean.

That is not putting off Jim Brittsan, though. “This is really exciting,” he says. Brittsan is the founder and executive director of coral restoration non-profit Sustainable Ocean and Reefs (SOAR). He is also the diver who arranged the temporary coral nursery beside the residence, having brought the corals from a site where, 10 metres closer to the surface, they faced increasing environmental stress. Now, in reduced temperatures, they are starting to flourish, hosting their own marine life – visible day and night, in all its busyness, from the underwater residence known as Vanguard just 15 metres away.

Vanguard is a long-stay underwater station for marine biologists. It was deployed in June 2026 at Tennessee Reef on the seafloor of the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, around 8 kilometres south of Long Key. Its coral nursery looks like a strange marine shrubbery: the coral fragments are arranged on anchored ropes that stand upright in the water. Once Vanguard is operational, a more permanent nursery will be established and the corals will eventually be planted on the seabed as part of ongoing restoration efforts, with their long-term survival assessed through monitoring.
Resident scientists will be able to monitor marine life around the clock

DEEP, the international design and engineering organisation that built Vanguard, aims to make humans aquatic by establishing more subsea habitats like it. These will allow people to live underwater for extended periods to engage in scientific research and conservation. This opens up unprecedented opportunities to do research because there is no need for divers to bounce up and down to a research vessel on the surface. Those round trips eat into valuable work hours, because divers can spend only limited time at depth and must ascend slowly to avoid decompression sickness. “If we’re diving from a boat, we can do about 3 hours’ work a day at depth,” Brittsan says. “It’s much more efficient if we can just stay down there.”

There is plenty of work to do in the Florida Keys. Elkhorn (Acropora palmata) and staghorn (Acropora cervicornis) corals, which are vital reef-building species, are now considered functionally extinct in Florida. But it is not just in Florida waters that corals are struggling. Climate change, which brings elevated ocean temperatures, is a significant threat to corals around the world. In warmer waters, corals eject the algae that live in their tissues. This upends their mutually beneficial symbiosis in what is known as a bleaching event – without the algae and other symbionts, the corals are left a ghostly white. If temperatures do not fall and the algae do not return, the corals eventually die.

In September 2026, amid concerns about marine heat stress, SOAR received authorisation to relocate 11 different coral species to the new nursery next to Vanguard. The corals were transported using different methods depending on the species: acroporid corals were transferred submerged in bins of seawater, while other corals were moved encased in seawater-soaked bubble wrap and placed in temperature-controlled coolers. The corals were then placed in the temporary nursery in deeper water near Vanguard.

Vanguard should be fully commissioned early in 2027. After that, those transplanted corals, and their attending creatures, can be continuously monitored by aquanauts who will be living in the habitat for a week at a time.

Brittsan and his team have also observed juvenile long-spined sea urchins (Diadema antillarum) that naturally recruited to Vanguard. “A lot of Diadema have started settling all over the habitat,” he says. This species of sea urchin is considered a keystone because its grazing reduces algal cover on reefs, providing space for corals and other reef organisms to settle and grow. That is why DEEP is taking a holistic approach, also planning to build sponge nurseries outside the habitat, for instance. “You need corals, sponges, sea urchins and everything else,” says Thomas Potts, science program director at DEEP.

Diadema urchins are particularly active at night, which means short daytime dives would miss a lot of what needs monitoring. “That’s where Vanguard really comes into play,” Potts says. Resident scientists will be able to monitor marine life around the clock.

The lessons from Vanguard will inform marine research in the Florida Keys for years to come. Vanguard is also a proving ground for DEEP’s future habitats. “It’s a great place to train scientists that might be working in different habitats on the continental shelf,” says Potts. The longer-term vision is to build a fleet of undersea residences at other locations. “This could be replicated throughout the Florida Keys and even in other parts of the world,” Brittsan says. “It’ll be a game-changer.”

Living among the species you are studying can provide deep insights, according to marine scientist Dr Steve Gittings. “We all know that if you really want to get to know a place, you should go and live there,” he says.

Gittings spent 27 years as chief scientist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Office of National Marine Sanctuaries. In that time, he spent many weeks living on Aquarius Reef Base, an ocean-floor habitat used for vital marine surveys. One of the biggest advantages of living underwater, he says, is that it creates a deeper appreciation of the wide variety of phenomena that contribute to a healthy reef. “There’s millions of things going on that are super-critical.”

But it is not just a useful path to deeper insights: it is a transformative experience. An extended stay in the ocean changes people in the same way that astronauts are changed after living in space. “There’s an emotional connection to living underwater that keeps you dedicated and committed,” Gittings says. That is why he is so excited about the inspiration that Vanguard will give to the aquanauts who live there: they will gain an irrepressible, lasting desire to help nature heal itself by removing stressors where possible, he reckons. “Only nature can do the full restoration,” Gittings says. “Our role is to create the conditions that allow nature to do its thing.”

items.title: November 19, 2005: The day Roger Federer scored the only double bagel in the history of the Masters Cup/ATP Finals
paras: Every day Tennis Majors takes you back in time to celebrate a great moment in tennis history. Today, we go back to 2005 to witness how Roger Federer blanked Gaston Gaudio, 6-0, 6-0, in the semi-finals of the ATP Masters Cup

At the end of 2005, Roger Federer had become world No 1, fulfilling the vast potential that many had seen in the young Swiss as a junior and fledgling pro. After he finished 1998 as world No 1 in juniors, Federer performed well in his first professional matches: in his five first main tour appearances, in 1998-1999, he reached the quarter-finals three times, in Toulouse, Marseille and Rotterdam.

Federer’s mind-blowing game amazed, and it was a swift rise that took him to No 1. The Swiss, very emotional during his first years on the tour, eventually mastered his nerves in 2003, when he claimed his first major title at Wimbledon (defeating Mark Philippoussis in the final, 7-6, 6-2, 7-6).
items.impact: A few months later, after triumphing at the Australian Open (defeating Marat Safin in the final, 7-6, 6-4, 6-3), he rose to No 1 on February 2, 2004.

items.title: Flavio Cobolli in tears during press conference following defeat to Frances Tiafoe, ‘I’m sad’
paras: Flavio Cobolli is already out of this year’s ATP Finals, following last night’s defeat to Frances Tiafoe. This marked his first-ever appearance at this prestigious end-of-year event, and he kickstarted it with a battling loss to Daniil Medvedev.

Such a defeat was hardly worrying, and in all honesty, it felt like his campaign hinged massively on his showdown with the American superstar, as a fellow first-timer. Whether it be fatigue, pressure, or something else entirely, Cobolli completely collapsed, and despite leading by a break in the first set, he would lose it on a tiebreak, before losing the second 6-0.

items.title: “Indoor hard courts should not be slow”: Medvedev takes a side in the court speed debate
paras: Asked in Turin about the court speed debate at the ATP Finals, the Russian made one exception to his love of variety after losing to Carlos Alcaraz, and explained why surface speed still matters against the Spaniard, even if he wins everywhere. Daniil Medvedev is all for variety in court speeds, but on one point he takes a side: indoor hard courts “should not be slow”.

The Russian, speaking at the ATP Finals in Turin after his 6-2, 6-4 defeat by Carlos Alcaraz , wants them fast, “a bit like here, a bit maybe like Paris was”. The question came from a journalist, who pointed to the debate this week, with some calling the surface too fast and others too slow.

Medvedev answered by defending variety above everything else. “I think definitely, the more different surfaces we have, the better it is, because everyone likes different courts, different balls,” he said.

items.title: What has become clear about Carlos Alcaraz after his victory against Daniil Medvedev in Turin
paras: Carlos Alcaraz continued his ATP Finals extravaganza on Wednesday afternoon, comfortably defeating Daniil Medvedev in his second group-stage match. The Spaniard beat Medvedev 6-2, 6-4 and has improved his record to 2-0 at the finals.

Alcaraz has also now collected seven victories at the ATP Finals – the joint-fifth most among active players. It was a particularly impressive victory for the 23-year-old due to the fact that he battled a left thigh issue during the match .

If Alcaraz’s issue proves to be minor, only one conclusion can be drawn about his campaign so far. Carlos Alcaraz is the world number three, trailing Alexander Zverev and Jannik Sinner in the rankings. Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
